subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Studying Atmospheres with JWST
description: A 60-second lesson on Studying Atmospheres with JWST.

hook.text: JWST is transforming exoplanet atmosphere science. Its infrared instruments detect molecules invisible to earlier telescopes.

buildup.text: It has already detected water, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide in exoplanet atmospheres with stunning clarity.

discovery.text: On WASP-39b, JWST produced the most detailed exoplanet spectrum ever—revealing photochemistry driven by its star's light.

twist.text: JWST can study smaller, cooler planets too. It's targeting rocky worlds in habitable zones for the first time.

climax.text: Early results from TRAPPIST-1 planets suggest some may lack thick atmospheres—a sobering but crucial finding.

punchline.text: Infrared eyes on alien skies. Every spectrum rewrites what we know.

quiz.question: What is JWST's advantage for studying exoplanet atmospheres?
options: Its infrared instruments detect molecules invisible to earlier telescopes
It can land probes on exoplanets to sample their atmospheres
It orbits close enough to exoplanets to photograph their surfaces

details.summary: JWST is revolutionizing exoplanet atmospheric science with its unprecedented infrared sensitivity. It has made the first detection of carbon dioxide in an exoplanet atmosphere, identified photochemistry through sulfur dioxide detection, and is characterizing small rocky worlds.
details.whyItMatters: JWST is the most powerful tool ever built for understanding what exoplanets are made of. Its observations are transforming theoretical models into measured properties for dozens of worlds.
takeaways: First detection of CO₂ and photochemistry in exoplanet atmospheres
Unprecedented infrared sensitivity for atmospheric characterization
Can study planets from hot gas giants to small rocky worlds

faq.question: Can JWST detect habitable conditions on rocky exoplanets?
faq.answer: Potentially, for nearby systems like TRAPPIST-1. JWST can detect or rule out thick CO₂ atmospheres on habitable zone rocky planets. Detecting water vapor or biosignatures on truly Earth-like planets is at the margin of JWST's capability — it may require hundreds of hours of observation per target.

faq.question: How many exoplanet atmospheres has JWST characterized?
faq.answer: In its first two years, JWST has published atmospheric detections for over a dozen exoplanets, ranging from hot Jupiters to rocky worlds. Highlights include WASP-39b (CO₂, SO₂, photochemistry), WASP-18b (thermal emission mapping), and TRAPPIST-1 b and c (ruling out thick atmospheres).
